description: We are LAGRANGE V, a team of five passionate about technology and space exploration. We bring together coding, software development, virtual reality, and communication to turn ideas into practical solutions. Our project, MarsPath, focuses on supporting Mars exploration through an engaging, interactive experience. We value teamwork, creativity, and learning together.
summary:
MarsPath is a working mission-planning and virtual-reality prototype developed by LAGRANGE V for the Martian Map challenge. Using NASA mission data, including HiRISE elevation and imagery distributed by USGS, it reconstructs a 10 × 10 km region of Jezero Crater. Users freely select a start and destination within this region and compare five route priorities: balanced, safest, fastest, science-focused, and energy-efficient. Route comparisons show distance, elevation changes, slope, estimated travel time, and modeled resource demand.

A laptop serves as Mission Control and sends the chosen route to a Meta Quest 3 headset. The astronaut explores the terrain with head tracking and controller-based movement, while the laptop follows progress and the astronaut’s view in real time. Terrain warnings, modeled oxygen and power estimates, and two-way voice communication support coordination.

By connecting terrain data, route planning, and immersive rehearsal, MarsPath helps teams understand exploration trade-offs and practice collaborative decisions before a simulated Mars traverse.
details:
Project purpose and experience

MarsPath is a working prototype developed by LAGRANGE V for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It connects terrain-aware mission planning on a laptop with an astronaut’s immersive navigation experience on Meta Quest 3.

Users explore a global Mars view, then select a start and destination freely within the supported 10 × 10 km Jezero Crater region. A Belva Crater showcase provides a prepared starting point for demonstrations. The application compares five route priorities: Balanced, Safest, Fastest, Science Priority, and Energy Efficient. Each alternative includes distance, estimated travel time, ascent and descent, maximum sampled track grade, and an elevation profile.

Terrain data and route calculation

The detailed Jezero terrain uses the USGS Mars 2020 TRN HiRISE elevation mosaic and matching orthorectified imagery, derived from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter observations. The elevation source has a native 1 m grid; selected image windows retain 0.25 m imagery. Global context uses products including MOLA topography and Viking imagery. Mars Trek supported source exploration and geographic comparison.

The C# routing engine constructs a terrain graph with eight-connected movement, elevation changes, valid-data checks, and configurable slope restrictions. Balanced uses A* with distance and modeled risk. Safest uses lexicographic Dijkstra to prioritize modeled risk, then distance. Fastest uses A* to minimize three-dimensional distance, with travel time estimated separately. Science Priority uses stage-expanded A* through ordered candidate stops. Energy Efficient uses A* with estimated electrical-energy costs.

Mission Control and astronaut coordination

The laptop operator selects a route and dispatches it to the waiting headset. The astronaut begins stationary and holds the right trigger to walk; releasing it stops movement. Head tracking allows natural exploration, while Mission Control follows route progress, geographic position, heading, and the astronaut’s view.

Two-way push-to-talk supports communication between the operator and astronaut. The laptop can inspect alternative routes and return to the live view during a traverse. Bundled Jezero data supports offline operation, with connected sessions using authorized USB or a compatible local Wi-Fi network.

Resource estimates and terrain warnings

The engineering model separates human metabolism from suit electrical consumption. It uses signed terrain grades, a Mars reference gravity of 3.71 m/s², gravitational work, the Weir calorimetry relationship for estimated oxygen demand, and an electrical-energy balance for battery depletion.

Slope warnings use elevation-derived terrain gradients. Rock warnings count visible modeled rocks ahead. Individual rock geometry and placement are illustrative; they are not surveyed obstacle locations. Suit parameters, warning thresholds, and resource estimates require further calibration before operational use.

Benefits, creativity, and intended impact

MarsPath brings map-based planning, resource trade-offs, immersive rehearsal, and live team coordination into one shared experience. Users can compare alternatives and experience their terrain consequences from the astronaut’s perspective.

The intended impact is to support education, exploration research, and collaborative mission rehearsal. The project encourages teams to consider elevation, resource demand, and science opportunities alongside distance when discussing a traverse.

Tools and design considerations

Development used Unity, C#, OpenXR, Meta Quest 3, Windows, Android, QGIS, Python, Git, and Git LFS. Design considerations included source coverage and uncertainty, Mars coordinate systems, physical elevation scale, headset performance, storage limits, readable interfaces, controlled movement, and connectivity.

Use of SI tools

OpenAI Codex assisted with brainstorming, research, data interpretation, coding, debugging, documentation, and interface development. Image generation produced illustrative terrain-warning icons, and synthetic text-to-speech provided the demo’s English narration. SI tools also supported demo scripting and production. Planetary terrain and orbital imagery come from credited source products. Runtime route calculation uses the documented graph-search algorithms.
